#5577. 10 flu shot myths and what the CDC said about them

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A 2011 gallery paired 12 flu vaccine fears with CDC answers. Here are 10 of those myths and what the agency said.

Flu season hands millions of Americans a small, personal choice. The decision takes a moment at a clinic, yet it rests as much on what people believe about the vaccine as on anything a doctor says. A person who trusts the shot books an appointment. A person who doubts it postpones the visit or skips it. Multiply those private calculations across the country, and beliefs about a single injection shape how families face the weeks ahead. The outcome touches more than the person in the chair. Coworkers, classmates, and relatives breathe the same air through those weeks.

Three worries keep surfacing as people weigh the shot. Some people fear the vaccine could trigger autism. Others suspect the shot delivers the illness it promises to prevent. A third group questions whether the injection accomplishes much of anything. Each fear carries a price. A parent worried about autism may keep a child unvaccinated. Someone convinced the needle brings on sickness may go without protection. A skeptic who sees no benefit has no reason to make the trip. Hesitation can also push the question down a crowded to-do list, where it can sit untouched. Answering these fears means setting each claim beside what public health authorities said about it, one at a time.

CBS News took on these objections in a photo gallery posted Dec. 6, 2011, as influenza made its yearly return. The gallery placed 12 widely held notions about influenza vaccines next to the position of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Each entry pairs a short statement of the myth with a brief rebuttal. Its corrections cite research in general terms and name no researchers, trials, or sample sizes. The evidence here reflects the agency's stance as the outlet relayed it. This article examines 10 of the gallery's 12 myths. Every answer that follows describes what the agency said in 2011, and readers should check current guidance before acting on any of it.

Flu shots contained only inactivated viruses in the 2011 season, and the CDC held that particles in that condition could not infect anyone. People who expect the needle to deliver the disease it targets misjudge what goes into the syringe. A dose of disabled virus has no way to start a case of influenza.

Salt-water placebo shots exposed only two complaints unique to the flu vaccine, redness where the needle entered and a sore arm. Researchers gave one group the vaccine and another an injection of salt water, then compared what each set of people reported. Both differences stayed confined to the injection site, and neither resembles a bout of flu. By this measure, the shot's distinct toll amounted to a tender, reddened patch of skin.

The CDC reports that needle-delivered flu vaccines rely on either inactivated viruses that cannot infect or proteins drawn from an influenza virus. The agency states that a flu vaccine cannot cause flu.

Flublok, a recombinant vaccine, comes from an insect cell line and uses no influenza viruses or eggs, according to the CDC. Flucelvax begins with influenza viruses grown in cell culture, which undergo inactivation and leave the finished product unable to give anyone influenza. The agency rules out influenza from either product. The two take separate paths to the same safety, one disabling the virus after growing it and the other never using it. Whatever the method of manufacture, none of these injected vaccines contains a virus able to cause disease.

Influenza that surfaces soon after a shot traces to a virus caught from another source. A person who catches the virus ahead of vaccination, or during the window before the body builds its protection, can fall ill. The CDC explains that the vaccine plays no part in such a case. Someone who gets sick after a flu shot has more reason to retrace recent exposures than to blame the vaccine.

A belief common in 2011 held that a flu shot lost its point once November ended, and the CDC's answer rejected that cutoff. Vaccination after that month kept paying off as long as influenza moved through communities. The myth turned a missed appointment into a reason to skip the whole season. Circulating virus set the real deadline.

Experts urged people to get immunized as soon as the vaccine became available that year. Early beat late, and late beat never. The advice named an early target without closing the door on later appointments. Anyone who missed the first weeks of supply had not lost the winter. The guidance treated a delayed shot as a fallback worth taking, and it gave no one grounds to pass on protection over a slow start.

Flu activity in the U.S. can begin climbing in October and hold on until May, according to the CDC. The CDC reports that activity tends to crest between December and February. Measured against that calendar, the heaviest stretch of illness arrives after the myth's supposed deadline has passed. Anyone who abandoned the shot under that logic would face the entire peak window unprotected.

The CDC repeated the point in its guidance for the 2022-2023 season, telling people who could not get vaccinated until November or later to go ahead at that point. The agency tied that advice to flu activity that can stay heavy into May. The agency's stance from 2011 held up in that later advice, and November offered no excuse to stay unvaccinated.

Early doses gave the fullest coverage, and later doses bought defense for the months when flu reached its height. A tardy start cost some weeks of protection without wiping out the payoff. By the myth's logic, the people most in need of a push, those already running behind, were the ones told to give up.

Last season's flu shot offered no promise of protection in 2011, according to the CDC position the gallery relayed. The gallery aimed that correction at people who believed a single shot keeps working for years. Flu viruses mutate from one year to the next, and each round of change leaves the previous formula a step behind. As a result, the vaccine got a fresh update every year. Anyone counting on a 2010 shot to carry them through the winter relied on a formula built for viruses that had since changed.

The slow pileup of small genetic mutations in influenza viruses goes by the name antigenic drift. The CDC's Pink Book identifies drift as the chief reason a person can catch influenza more than once. The same process explains why the makeup of flu vaccines faces review and revision each year. Each new recipe answers a virus that refuses to hold still.

Immunity from any one shot fades in less than a year for practical purposes, according to the Pink Book. Two forces drive the decline. The antibodies a vaccine prompts the body to make wane, and the circulating viruses keep drifting away from the strains the shot aimed at.

Strain match governs how much benefit a shot delivers. The payoff varies with the resemblance between vaccine strains and the strains spreading in a given season. Three other factors shape the result: the recipient's age, the recipient's health, and the type of vaccine. A shot designed around an earlier season's viruses starts behind on strain match. The strains it targets have had another year to evolve.

Yearly reformulation and the brief life of vaccine immunity turn the flu shot into a seasonal appointment. Each season resets the question, and the only shot that answers it is the one built for the viruses circulating that winter.

Government scientists in 2011 urged vaccinated people to keep up the everyday steps that stop germs and viruses, including those behind influenza, from moving between people. Under that guidance, a flu shot excused no one from ordinary hygiene. The myth treats vaccination as the last step anyone needs, and the 2011 position answered it by keeping those steps in place after the shot.

Tiny drops of fluid make the case for those routines. Experts believe the main way flu travels between people is through drops an infected person releases by coughing, sneezing, or speaking. Those drops can land in the mouth or nose of someone close by, who may breathe them into the lungs as well. A second, less common route runs through objects. Someone touches a surface holding flu virus and then touches the mouth or nose, and in some cases the eyes.

Feeling healthy offers no proof of being harmless to others. A person with flu may be able to pass the virus along before realizing they are sick, as well as during the illness. Silent spread gives daily safeguards a job on days a vaccinated person feels fine.

A few plain practices close off those paths. Covering the nose and mouth during a cough or sneeze might shield people nearby from illness. Keeping distance from others can lower the odds of handing a respiratory virus along. Regular handwashing protects against germs, and an alcohol-based hand rub fills in when soap and water are out of reach. Clean hands target the object route, where germs reach the eyes, nose, or mouth on a person's own fingers.

Government scientists asked parents to teach the same habits to their children, a request that extended the recommendation past the vaccinated adult and into the rest of the household. A shot works inside one body. Covered coughs, distance, and washed hands interrupt the trips flu takes between bodies, and the 2011 advice relied on both layers at once.

Holding off on a flu shot until people nearby fell sick opened a gap of about two weeks, the time the vaccine needed to deliver full protection under the CDC's position as of 2011. The myth cast vaccination as a response to someone else's illness. Its believers figured they needed a shot only once the flu had reached the people around them. Under that logic, a symptom-free social circle served as proof that the needle could wait.

Sick neighbors make a poor alarm. Waiting for others to fall ill was likely to mean acting too late, the CDC held. By the time a cough moves through an office or a household, the virus is circulating within arm's reach, and the person who held off has no head start. A visible case marks a moment when exposure may already have occurred. Symptoms in others tell a person about the past, and a vaccine plan built on them trails the virus.

Antibodies that guard against flu need that same stretch to form after vaccination, according to the CDC. A shot taken after a local wave of illness begins leaves its recipient unshielded during the window when the virus moves through family, friends, and coworkers. The body spends those days building its response while the virus keeps moving.

The myth also misreads what a flu shot does. Vaccination works by preparing the body before a threat appears. A flu shot behaves the way a smoke detector does, useful only if someone mounts it before the fire starts. Treating it as an emergency response turns a preventive tool into a gamble on timing.

The cost of delay lands on the person who waited. Each day spent watching others for signs of illness eats into the lead time the vaccine requires. Timing the vaccine to a local outbreak reverses the order that matters. Immunity has to be in place before exposure. The decision to get a shot belongs ahead of the first sniffle in anyone nearby.

Babies younger than six months can catch influenza, yet in 2011 the CDC considered them too young to receive a flu shot. The myth assumes anyone at risk can roll up a sleeve. Infants in their first half-year break that assumption. They face the virus with no vaccine of their own to stop it. Age alone kept the shot from them. Nothing in the CDC's answer suggested these babies resisted infection.

The CDC's 2011 remedy moved the defense one step outward. Its best safeguard for these infants was immunization for every other member of the household, along with the caregivers who tend the child. Parents, older siblings, and babysitters all fall inside that circle. A grandparent who watches the baby on weekends belongs in it as well. Each vaccinated person closes one route the virus could travel to reach the baby.

The guidance turns a personal health choice into a family one. An adult who skips the shot leaves a gap in the barrier around a child who cannot get one. With no shot to fall back on, the infant relies on coverage among the grown-ups to set the level of safety in the home. The circle can defend the baby no better than its weakest member allows.

Daily habits shield infants from flu alongside the vaccine. Keeping babies away from sick people and disinfecting surfaces both help. Covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue, wearing a mask, and washing hands the right way add more layers. The adults carry out all of those steps. A baby cannot wash its own hands, wear a mask, or step away from a coughing visitor. Even the protection that comes without a needle depends on the people nearby.

Each adult's decision about the vaccine in 2011 counted twice in a home with a young infant, once for the adult and once for the baby.

A flu shot could lower a person's chance of catching influenza by as much as 90%, according to the CDC position the gallery relayed in 2011. The agency paired that figure with a concession. The vaccine does not succeed every time. The two statements fit together. Studies put 90% at the ceiling of what the shot can achieve, and some recipients land below it. A person weighing the shot was buying a lower risk, with no guarantee attached.

Older adults and young children gain less from the vaccine, the CDC said in 2011. Age is one of several traits that shape the shot's results. Flu vaccine effectiveness can shift with a person's underlying medical conditions, past bouts of influenza, and earlier vaccinations. A healthy adult and an older relative with chronic illness can receive the same dose and come away with unequal defense.

Serious flu complications remain a target the shot can hit in cases where it fails to block infection, according to the 2011 guidance. An older adult or young child who comes down with the flu despite vaccination may avoid the worst turns of the illness. The benefit narrows in those groups without disappearing. A better match between the vaccine and the viruses spreading in a community raises the odds of strong protection against influenza illness and its complications.

Everyday conditions outside the controlled setting of a clinical trial can trim the payoff a vaccine provides. A figure drawn from a season of routine clinic visits can fall below the gallery's upper mark without contradicting it.

The myth grades the vaccine by the cases it fails to prevent. Judged that way, the shot looks weakest among older adults and young children, the same populations where the 2011 guidance credited it with heading off dangerous aftereffects. A tally of cases alone leaves out half the job the CDC assigned the shot for those patients.

Thimerosal, the ingredient behind the autism fear, showed no connection to the disorder across many studies, according to the CDC's position in 2011. The compound is a mercury-containing preservative, and some flu vaccines carried it that season. Critics had blamed it for a range of health problems and counted autism among them. The accusation pinned autism on a single component of a single shot, which handed researchers a narrow target to test.

Small doses of thimerosal caused no harm beyond redness and swelling at the injection site, the CDC's position held. Mercury on a vaccine ingredient list can alarm a parent, yet the amounts in a flu vaccine were small. The usual reactions stayed local, confined to the patch of skin around the needle. A few people may be allergic to thimerosal, though the CDC describes such reactions as rare. Critics described harm extending past the arm, and the evidence the agency relayed kept the common effects at the spot where the needle went in.

The no-link finding has outlasted the 2011 season. The CDC's vaccine-safety guidance concludes that research has turned up no connection between thimerosal in vaccines and autism. The agency points to numerous well-designed investigations that ruled out any role for the compound in causing the condition. Across the years between the 2011 gallery and the agency's current guidance, the answer on autism has held steady.

The fear hangs on one ingredient, and the findings left that ingredient with no case to answer. Thimerosal appeared in some 2011 flu vaccines and not in others. Versions without the preservative existed that season as well. A parent uneasy about mercury had a route to protection that left the compound out. A person who skipped vaccination over autism worries gave up immunity against influenza to avoid a danger the investigations never found. Of the two threats weighed in that choice, only influenza carried any evidence behind it.

Children between six months and eight years old who had never received a seasonal flu vaccine needed two doses at least four weeks apart in 2011, under the CDC's guidance at the time.

One vaccine covered the entire 2011 season, and most people needed a single dose of it. The gallery used those facts to puncture the idea that one shot leaves a person exposed. The myth takes a real rule and stretches it across the whole population, when the requirement applied to a narrow slice of young children.

The two-dose rule hinged on two conditions holding at once, the child's age and a blank vaccination record. An eight-year-old who had received a seasonal shot in a previous year fell outside it. So did a nine-year-old receiving a first flu shot. Age alone put that child past the cutoff.

The required spacing turns a young child's first flu season into a two-visit commitment, with the return trip landing a month or more after the first. Every week of delay on the opening shot pushes the follow-up back by the same week. A family that waits for a convenient moment to start the series also delays the day the child completes the course.

The CDC describes the first dose as a primer that readies the immune system, with the second dose delivering the actual protection. A child who needs both shots but receives one can end up with weaker protection or none, according to the CDC. Skipping the follow-up wastes much of what the first visit set in motion.

The CDC reports that children who have received two doses at any point need a single dose in the current season. The present-day test counts completed pairs of doses. The gallery's 2011 wording turned on whether a child had ever received a seasonal shot. Completing the pair in a child's first season sets up every one-shot season that follows.

Tamiflu and Relenza, two prescription-only antivirals, served as a backup against flu in the CDC position relayed in 2011, with the shot holding the front line. These drugs come as pills, liquids, and inhaled powders, and they treat the symptoms of an infection underway. Neither one can replace a vaccine that builds defenses before the virus arrives.

Speed decides whether these medicines help. In 2011, the guidance held that their benefit depended on a patient starting them within the first day or two of illness. Prompt treatment can ease the harshest flu effects and shorten the illness by an average of one day, according to the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The institute describes antiviral medicines as a way to help head off severe complications, including bacterial pneumonia. The early cutoff restricts their value to patients who seek care at the first signs of sickness.

A doctor's prescription stands between a patient and either drug. Pharmacies cannot sell flu antivirals without one. The medicines block influenza viruses from copying themselves inside the body. They act on influenza alone and offer nothing against other viruses that cause similar complaints. A patient with a flu-like illness who obtains a prescription may see no improvement from the drug if a different virus caused it. The visit needed to get that prescription can consume part of the brief period when the drugs work.

The CDC calls a yearly flu vaccine its first and most important step against flu and lists drugs to treat flu illness as another option. The agency's stance matches the order the 2011 gallery described, with antivirals waiting in reserve behind the shot. The vaccine aims to keep flu from taking hold. The medicines try to blunt a case in progress against a ticking clock. Anyone who skips the shot and counts on a prescription is betting on spotting the illness in time, reaching a doctor, and having influenza and not some other virus.

#5576. Ferrari’s Luce was ridiculed as a ‘Magic Mouse on wheels.’ Now the EV is sold out for 2027, and buyers haven’t even driven it yet

Ferrari’s first electric car sparked ridicule when it was unveiled on May 25. It was called any and everything from a ‘Magic Mouse on wheels’ to a dishwasher or microwave, and even considered a late April Fool’s joke by some fans. Even a former Ferrari president and chairman hoped the company would take off the prancing horse emblem from the Luce, saying Ferrari was “risking the destruction of a myth.”

It looks like that ridicule hasn’t stopped buyers: Ferrari’s Luce, with a $560,800 starting price, has a buyer for every car Ferrari plans to build in 2027, and wealthy buyers are lining up for the glass-roofed EV before they even get the chance to test drive it. CEO Benedetto Vigna told analysts on Ferrari’s Q3 earnings call on Tuesday that Luce deliveries for 2027 are all spoken for despite client test drives being planned for early next year.

“All the Luces that we plan to sell next year, basically, are all allocated, so if someone comes, he has to wait one year to get the cars,” Vigna said, though he didn’t mention how many units were sold.

Vigna also said Ferrari holding more than 50 local premieres and private viewings across the U.S., Europe, Middle East, and Asia Pacific has helped express Luce’s “uniqueness better than any digital experience.”

The early interest for Luce is a reversal from its rocky debut, when Ferrari shares fell by as much as 8% and analysts wondered whether the car’s unconventional design–larger wheels, more rounded surfaces, and four doors–rattled investors who valued Ferrari for its luxurious visual identity.

“While the vehicle promises performance consistent with Ferrari’s standards, investors appeared underwhelmed by its exterior design,” Rella Suskin, an equity analyst at Morningstar, wrote in a note after the release. “Ferrari’s design identity is an important component of its brand equity, supporting scarcity, pricing power, and aspirational desirability.”

But Vigna, who enlisted LoveFrom, the firm founded by former Apple design chief Jony Ive, to build Luce, has defended his breakaway from tradition. He told analysts on the Feb. 10 Q4 2025 earnings call that Luce wouldn’t please everyone, but that it’s still a Ferrari car first and EV second.

“What I can tell you, I can guarantee you is that we will not sell this car to people that do not want the car,” he said. “Because this is a car, Ferrari Luce, that is also electric. It’s not an electric car.”

Ferrari is also taking a gamble with Luce as its competitors are reconsidering their EV ambitions because of weaker demand. Lamborghini scrapped its plan to roll out its first fully electric car in 2028, and Porsche—which announced its first electric sports car Taycan seven years before Ferrari–is reportedly planning to end Taycan’s production by 2030. But Ferrari is pressing ahead with Luce—Italian for “light”—which Vigna described as “illuminating the path ahead” for the brand.

This innovation also comes as Ferrari’s core business continues to grow. The carmaker reported €1.9 billion in Q3 revenue, up 7% from a year earlier, and €563 million in operating profit, fueled partly by buyers spending more to customize their cars. CFO Antonio Picca Piccon told analysts personalization made up more than 21% of total revenues from cars and spare parts, which he said “exceeded our expectations.”

Ferrari did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

#5575. Millennial moms are facing pay cuts at exactly the moment they need to earn more

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Mothers rarely win back the pay they lose after a first child. Millennial women are having babies now, often without leave or day care to keep working

At 34, Alicia Adamczyk, senior editor of personal finance newsletter The Purse, said she'd reached the age when college-educated women see their raises peter out. She married later than women in past generations did, doesn't own a home yet, and is weighing whether to have children. Corinne Low, an economist at the Wharton School who studies gender and discrimination, explained to her that "women's earnings do tend to level off in their mid-30s."

"That's the pattern, that's the average," Low added, "but that's not destiny."

Women don't stall in their mid-30s because of their age. Men the same age keep pulling ahead of them. In 2010, women who were 25 to 34, including the oldest millennials, made about $93 for every $100 men their age earned per hour, according to Pew Research Center. Nine years later, their salaries fell nearly three times as far behind. Over those same years, many of them started caring for children or other relatives and cut back at work, while men their age didn't.

Women fall furthest behind after a first child. Millennial women are having their first children now, many of them while starting their careers over. They're cutting back at work in the same years they're trying to rebuild. The pay women give up in their 30s doesn't come back. Gen X $TWTR women hit their 30s a decade before millennials, and they still make about $80 for every $100 men their age earn.

American women in heterosexual relationships have their first child at about 29, on average, and within a year, they earn about a fifth less than they did before having their baby, according to a working paper by Census Bureau and RAND Corporation researchers, who tracked couples' earnings records from 2005 to 2021. By 34, Adamczyk's age, they barely win back any of the pay they lost. But their husbands keep getting the same raises they got before they became fathers, and as the years go by, more of the family's money comes from the husband.

Mothers cut their hours or leave their jobs when a first child arrives, even when they bring home more money than their husbands, according to the Census and RAND researchers.. Their husbands keep working the same hours and keep getting raises, and many of those families end up depending more on the fathers' pay than on the mothers'. Same-sex couples don't divide the work that way. Both parents keep working, and by the time their child starts school, the lower earner is often making more than before.

The researchers concluded that couples decide which parent cuts back by what they think mothers and fathers are supposed to do, not by who brings home the bigger paycheck. Harvard economist Claudia Goldin told Princeton University Press in 2021 that the mother usually becomes the parent the family can always reach. "Working mothers are 'on-call at home,'" Goldin said, "whereas working fathers are 'on-call at work.'"

Goldin says mothers wouldn't have to be the parent "on-call at home" if flexible hours and child care cost families less. "The route out of these inequities is to lower the cost of workplace flexibility and childcare," she said. Half of working parents don't even get paid time off from their jobs for a new child, a sick relative, or their own health, according to a Pew survey in March. When a baby arrives, one parent takes the time unpaid or leaves, and that parent is usually the mother.

When a child gets sick or day care closes early, mothers usually leave work to handle it. Goldin says they lose far more than missed hours. The best-paying jobs pay the most to workers available at any hour. "Doubling the time far more than doubles the earnings," she said. "That is what we call 'greedy work.'" Each time mothers leave work early, they fall further out of line for those raises. Fathers stay available and collect them. And when they become the biggest earners, their families have even more reason to keep the them at work the next time a child gets sick.

Some mothers eventually weigh what day care costs against what they now earn and decide to stay home. Low, the Wharton economist, told Adamczyk that the choice "is not about the spot price right now versus your wages right now," because by leaving the workforce, mothers give up the "career growth that might increase your work-life balance later."

Millennial mothers are choosing now between unpaid time off and leaving their jobs. Without paid leave, many more will quit, saving a few years of day care bills while giving up raises for the rest of their careers.

#5574. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5573. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5572. Billionaires Ray Dalio and Richard Branson hate workplace gossip—but men who do it could face a steeper career penalty than women, study finds

Men who gossip around the office watercooler could be hurting their chances of climbing the corporate ladder.

That’s according to a new study by researchers at the University of Iowa and the University of New Mexico, which found that men who gossip are perceived as less competent and less qualified for leadership roles than women who engage in the same behavior.

“Men when they engage in gossip, they tend to be judged a lot more harshly than women,” Trevor Spoelma, an associate professor of management and entrepreneurship at the University of Iowa’s Tippie College of Business, told Fortune.

The researchers reached that conclusion through three studies: an observation of 272 undergraduate students working in five-person teams on a class project, followed by two online experiments involving roughly 450 U.S. workers.

Across the studies, people who gossiped received lower competence ratings, but men faced a steeper penalty than women.

Gossip has existed as a social practice for centuries, but the word itself took on a more negative connotation around the 16th century, when it became increasingly associated with women spreading rumors. That history may help explain the gender double standard. When men gossip about a third party, they can be seen as violating traditional expectations of how men should behave, Spoelma said. For women, the behavior may be viewed as more consistent with longstanding gender stereotypes.

Negative gossip, Spoelma added, can involve questioning a colleague’s abilities, criticizing their work, or sharing an unflattering story about them. But gossip isn’t always necessarily malicious. It can also mean complimenting a colleague or sharing a harmless anecdote about someone who isn’t in the room.

In some cases, both forms of gossip can have benefits to employees by fostering trust and a sense of belonging.

“You’re suddenly in on something that supposedly not everyone’s in on. You become part of that inner circle,” psychologist Scott Lyons previously told Fortune. “You feel special. You feel like you matter.”

That sense of connection could be particularly valuable as hybrid work enables employees to collaborate less face-to-face. And amid a broader loneliness crisis among men, informal workplace interactions can offer another way to build meaningful relationships with colleagues.

But while men tend to receive more leniency than women when their behavior violates social norms or is perceived as unusual, gossip appears to be an exception, Spoelma said.

“A lot of times, men receive a pass compared to women for different norm-violating behaviors,” he told Fortune. “But specifically, when it comes to gossip, that’s an instance where we see this penalty.”

Despite employees enjoying gossip, some of the world’s most prominent business leaders have made clear they don’t think it has a place in the workplace.

Billionaire co-founder of Virgin Group Richard Branson, for example, has long championed a philosophy of avoiding speaking poorly of others.

“If I ever hear anybody gossiping, I will walk away because it’s just not good,” he told LinkedIn in 2024.

“Everything comes back to people, people, people.“Are you good with people? Are you good at drawing out the best in people?”

Ray Dalio, the billionaire founder of hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, has echoed that talking about people behind their backs in the workplace is counterproductive.

“You shouldn’t talk behind somebody’s back or gossip,” he said in an interview with the Academy of Achievement in 2012.

“Too many people talk about the other people, what they’re doing wrong,” Dalio explained. “Except they don’t talk to those people about what they’re doing wrong. So they don’t know whether they’re actually doing them wrong or not. They haven’t heard the other side and they’re not being productive. So that’s terrible.”

Personal finance radio show host Dave Ramsey has gone so far to make “No Gossip” one of the 14 values of his company, Ramsey Solutions.

“One of our core values is, I will fire you for being a gossip. I just did it and I’ll do it again,” he said on his EntreLeadership show in 2024.

Workplace disagreements and frustrations are inevitable, Ramsey acknowledged, but employees have a responsibility not to make them worse by spreading negativity among colleagues.

“You have one option at Ramsey. You must hand your negatives up to someone in leadership who can do something about it,” he said. “But if you hand your negatives down or sideways, that’s called gossip. I’ll warn you once maybe, but we’ll probably just fire you.”

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5571. A WhatsApp channel called Lula’s Army grew from 50,000 to more than 10 million subscribers as Brazil’s president staged a historic comeback

A leader who stood up to U.S. President Donald Trump just won an election in Latin America’s biggest country, reversing a trend of new right-wing governments in the region over the past two years.

Incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, having narrowly lost to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of voting on Oct. 5, 2026, staged a remarkable comeback on Oct. 25. He erased the deficit and won the all-important runoff election by more than 3.5 percentage points – more than 4 million votes.

It was a stunning result for the leader who proved to be the first Brazilian candidate to win a presidential election after not winning the first round, and who had been all but written off for a possible win. As a professor of Latin American politics, I believe the result offers a number of key political lessons for Brazil, Latin America – and even the United States.

The choice in the second-round election was stark. Lula offered measures to ameliorate steep income inequalities and an economy built on a transition to clean energy, environmental protection and increased access to higher education and technical training. On international matters, Lula balanced defending Brazilian sovereignty from a Trump administration keen on meddling in Latin America, and maintaining good relations with an array of nations and blocs, including the European Union and China.

Bolsonaro, meanwhile, promised sweeping cuts to government spending, more militarized policing and eager support for the Trump administration’s campaign against drug violence. His pitch also came with offers to U.S. investors of access to critical minerals in Brazil.

Such right-wing populism has been ascendant in Latin America of late, and Lula also had to overcome an anti-incumbent mood, brought on by high prices, stagnant salaries, steep interest rates and a massive corruption scandal involving Brazilian elites. That banking probe directly ensnared Bolsonaro himself, as well as powerful Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes, whom Bolsonaro’s supporters had tried to link to Lula.

Lula also had to neuter a social media landscape that has been dominated by images and narratives disparaging the president and his Workers’ Party.

Right-wing dominance of that online ecosystem helped carry Jair Bolsonaro, the 2026 hopeful’s father, to power in 2018 and got him close to reelection in 2022.

Especially after the first-round results in the 2026 vote, many analysts assumed the same pro-Bolsonaro social media presence would once again be hegemonic.

Instead, after the first round, a network of young, tech-savvy pro-Lula communicators created and shared effective, often amusing videos on WhatsApp and Instagram.

And they appealed to the center and even some of the right. All told, Lula easily made up more than 2 million votes by which he lost in the first round. He didn’t just increase turnout by millions and lower abstention rates; he also saw the state with the country’s second-largest electorate, Minas Gerais, flip to his side entirely – a swing of nearly 700,000 votes.

The creator of the channel, André Janones, is a federal deputy for the Rede Party, an ally of the Workers’ Party, and a rising star in the circle around Lula. Likewise, Ana Elisa Santos Silva, a 21-year-old digital influencer and law student in the Workers’ Party, got the most votes of any federal deputy in the swing state of Minas Gerais.

A prevalent narrative of Brazilian politics has held that the country’s divisions increasingly mirror those of the United States.

Part of that idea is due to Trump’s loss in the 2020 election and the resulting attack on the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, which eerily presaged events following Jair Bolsanaro’s 2022 loss.

Like in the U.S., there has also been a rapid rise of a politically active evangelical right in Brazil.

More fundamentally, proponents of the Americanization thesis hold that U.S.-style deindustrialization and “Uberization” of the Brazilian economy have led to a decline of the unionized working class – a core support base for the left – and its replacement by an army of gig employees dreaming of owning their own businesses and throwing off the shackles of the taxing and regulating state.

Yet similarities between the two countries shouldn’t be confused for politics always moving on parallel tracks.

Survey research suggests that many Brazilians see the state as responsible for the realization of their constitutionally protected social rights, including healthcare, education and pensions. Many also regard government employment as inherently more stable and dignified than the harsh labor markets of the private sector, especially for the relatively unskilled.

For all of the apparent rise in American-style libertarian politics in Brazil, the reality is that such a viewpoint remains much smaller in the country. Flávio Bolsonaro’s bet, like his father’s before him, was that this strain of libertarian right-wing politics could nonetheless propel him to victory, much as it apparently had for Javier Milei in Argentina in 2023. But it was not enough.

Even with Lula’s win, Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party did exceptionally well at the legislative level.

When the next Brazilian Congress convenes on Feb. 1, 2027, the Liberal Party will control 28 seats in the Senate – 35% of the total; and 121 seats in the lower house – 24% of the total (as well as five governorships, which are 19% of the total).

When factoring in expected Liberal Party allies, it is clear that the right will have bigger majorities in both houses for Lula’s next administration. That will help Congress solidify control vis-a-vis the executive branch in terms of legislation and, crucially, the budget.

First, it is unclear how Lula, who will turn 81 on Oct. 27, will be able to effectively govern. The president will have to make major concessions to a Congress with little capacity for responsibly delivering coherent policy.

The federal Supreme Court is also seen as politicized, fragmented and tainted by scandals. On the other hand, Lula could appoint four new Supreme Court justices because of upcoming retirements, meaning that he could shape the country’s highest judicial body in a way that enhances his ability to manage Congress.

Yet it might be difficult for Lula to simultaneously meet the demands coming from Congress and those from the business community. For example, many will push the government to curb the fiscal deficit, currently running at a very high annual level of close to 8% of gross domestic product.

A second question is whether Bolsonaro’s loss will splinter the right. One interpretation of the 2026 election is that to be competitive, the right will want to move on from the Bolsonaro family. One potential figure is Tarcísio de Freitas, a former cabinet member in the Jair Bolsonaro government and popular governor of São Paulo. Yet there are nonetheless five members of the Bolsonaro family in the new Congress, and they are likely to try to keep together the coalition that fought for Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign.

Finally, it’s not clear how the Trump administration, which interfered decisively against Lula’s agenda, will react to his win – and to what extent it will support Bolsonaro’s denial of his election loss even though it was bigger than his father’s in 2022.

Whatever the extent of any interference, the Trump administration’s right-wing Latin American vision invariably sets up conflict with Lula. Yet while the Trump preference was always for Flávio Bolsonaro, that doesn’t mean his administration won’t pragmatically engage with Lula even as it pressures his government. For his part, Lula continues to hold his own leverage, including through Brazil’s large deposits of rare earth elements that the Trump administration covets.

If the past eight years of Brazilian politics are any guide, Lula’s next administration is likely to be a turbulent one in which enduring divisions at home and abroad are continually tested.

Anthony W. Pereira, Executive Director of the Stone Center for Latin American Studies, Tulane University; King’s College London

#5570. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

#5569. Florida voters nearly tripled the homeowner tax break — blowing an $11.8 billion hole in county budgets

Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes.

Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis.

But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments.

While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off.

Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes.

In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses.

So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters.

Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits.

But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached.

Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments.

With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups.

This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages.

State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees.

Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event.

In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties.

And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll.

Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing.

When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall.

From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs.

Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift.

This article has been corrected to note that the current homestead exemption is $51,400 and that new Florida residents who buy a home are eligible for a property tax break on a phased-in basis.

Portions of this article appeared in a prior article published on July 30, 2026.

Abigail Hall, Professor of Economics, University of Tampa and Aaron D. Wood, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Tampa

#5567. Microsoft opens Imagine Cup to startups, and the new rules show how its AI strategy has changed

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 8:04 amNovember 3, 2026 at 8:09 am

Microsoft’s Imagine Cup, a competition for student developers since 2003, is expanding for the first time to early-stage startups whose founders aren’t in school, with $250,000 in cash and $1 million in cloud credits awarded to the winner.

The change, announced Monday, opens the competition to companies founded in the past two years that haven’t raised a Series C round, whether or not their founders are students.

Startups will compete in six industry categories, including cybersecurity, developer tools and healthcare. Students will get a seventh category of their own, with a $25,000 top prize, or they can choose to compete for the main prize in the industry categories.

It’s the latest step in a broader evolution of the Imagine Cup, and the implications go beyond the competition itself. Changes in the rules from 2024 to 2027 show how Microsoft and the tech industry are adjusting, year by year, to the realities of the AI era.

Changing AI requirements: The clearest example is the Imagine Cup rules for AI usage. In 2024, entrants had to build their products with “Microsoft and/or OpenAI” services. In 2025, they had to use at least one Microsoft AI service. In 2026, they had to use at least two Microsoft AI services.

For 2027, they can use any AI they want, as long as they use Microsoft’s Azure cloud.

The shift mirrors a broader change in Microsoft’s AI strategy. The company has added models from Anthropic, xAI, Meta and others to Azure. In April it ended its exclusive cloud arrangement with its longtime AI partner OpenAI, allowing the ChatGPT maker to sell its technology through other platforms such as Amazon Web Services.

Microsoft Foundry, the company’s platform for building AI applications, offers access to more than 11,000 models.

“Imagine Cup 2027 reflects that same approach, giving founders the flexibility to choose the right models and technologies for their solutions while meeting the competition’s Azure and technical requirements,” said Tom Davis, general manager of Microsoft for Startups, in a statement responding to GeekWire’s questions.

Why startups: Addressing the expansion to non-student startups, Davis said AI is letting more founders start companies faster than ever, and the revamped competition is meant to help those young companies win customers and prepare to sell to big businesses.

The judging criteria have changed to match that focus on business customers.

As recently as 2024, student teams couldn’t have raised more than $50,000 in outside funding to compete. Under the new rules, final-round judges, whose scores determine all of the winners, will look for net revenue retention over the previous 12 months, six months of traction data, and a customer reference willing to be contacted.

What’s in it for Microsoft: The change is also a way for Microsoft to bring promising startups onto Azure. For startups in the industry categories, the first-round scoring criteria in 2027 will include “Microsoft and Azure commercial readiness, and expected cloud and AI consumption.”

Azure gets less explicit weight in the final round, whose scores determine the winners. A live production workload on Azure is worth 6 of 100 points there. In 2026, use of Microsoft technology made up 40% of the score in every round.

Participants can also earn Azure credits by using more of Microsoft’s cloud services. The credits start at $1,000 and rise to as much as $150,000 for startups that run at least 10 eligible Azure workloads and spend $3,000 a month on Azure for 60 days.

Amazon and Google run their own credit programs for startups, as the cloud giants compete to win AI companies early, when they’re choosing where to build.

Diversity criteria dropped: The new rules also drop diversity, inclusion and accessibility from the judging criteria, where they had been through 2026. In 2024, inclusion was worth 10% of the score, with judges asked to consider factors such as gender, ethnicity and disability.

Davis said Microsoft “updated the judging framework to reflect the range of industries and customer challenges represented in the competition,” and that inclusion and accessibility remain central to the company’s mission. He added that the competition welcomes startups developing products focused on inclusion and accessibility.

Separately, Microsoft skipped its annual diversity report last year, ending a tradition it started in 2019, as Google, Meta, Amazon and other big tech companies scaled back diversity programs under pressure from the Trump administration.

Prizes and timing: Applications are due Feb. 28. The second-place startup will receive $50,000 and $350,000 in credits, and third place gets $25,000 and $350,000 in credits. The 2026 champion, CopyFlag, a U.K. startup that tracks copies of creators’ designs online, won $150,000.

The top startup in the student category will present at the World Championship but isn’t eligible for the top three prizes, according to the official rules. To compete for those top prizes, student startups can enter an industry category instead, going up against companies that may have raised as much as a Series B.

The rules also allow Microsoft to use “automated assistance” to triage, summarize and compare entries, with human review in advancement decisions.

Winners will be selected in April and announced in May or June at a World Championship, with the date and location still to be determined, Davis said. The 2026 finale was at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in San Francisco.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5566. Why Entrepreneurs Need to Stop Carrying Everything to Keep Their Business Growing

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Entrepreneurs are celebrated for how much responsibility they can handle. But as businesses grow, carrying everything can become the very thing holding them back.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Entrepreneurs are often praised for their ability to carry enormous responsibility. They build companies, manage employees, serve customers, make payroll and navigate uncertainty, sometimes all before lunch.

In the beginning, carrying everything can feel necessary. You become the salesperson, marketer, accountant and customer service department because there’s nobody else to do it.

But something changes as the business grows. The responsibilities multiply, and the habits that helped you survive the startup phase can become obstacles to sustainable success.

You may have built a thriving business while becoming exhausted, disconnected from your family or unable to imagine the company functioning without you.

The problem isn’t necessarily that you’re carrying too much. It’s that you haven’t reconsidered what you’re carrying, why you’re carrying it and whether it’s still yours to carry.

That’s the thinking behind a framework I call The Five Carries.

Entrepreneurial ambition can make overextension feel like commitment. Yet research suggests that passion alone doesn’t protect founders from exhaustion.

A study discussed in Harvard Business Review examined how entrepreneurial passion, work characteristics and beliefs about success relate to burnout. Its findings challenge the assumption that loving your business automatically makes relentless work sustainable.

The pressure extends beyond founders. Gallup’s State of the Global Workplace 2026 report found that global manager engagement declined from 31% in 2022 to 22% in 2025. Managers, like entrepreneurs, frequently navigate competing expectations without sufficient capacity to meet them.

The lesson isn’t that responsibility should be avoided. It’s that responsibility must be managed intentionally.

The Five Carries framework organizes those responsibilities into five directions.

Entrepreneurs may not have traditional bosses, but they still answer to investors, lenders, boards, customers and their own ambitions.

Carry Up involves managing those expectations without allowing them to dictate every decision.

Consider a founder who promises aggressive expansion to investors while privately recognizing that the team lacks the resources to deliver. Carrying up effectively means communicating reality, negotiating priorities and setting responsible expectations rather than making commitments the business cannot sustain.

Ask yourself: Whose expectations am I carrying, and have I agreed to more than I can responsibly deliver?

Leadership sometimes requires the courage to disappoint someone today to protect the business tomorrow.

Employees depend on business owners for direction, resources, opportunities and a working environment where they can succeed.

But carrying down doesn’t mean absorbing everyone’s problems.

A founder who personally resolves every employee challenge may feel indispensable while unintentionally preventing the team from developing independence.

Effective leadership involves providing clarity, coaching and accountability so others become increasingly capable.

Instead of asking, “How can I solve this for my team?” consider asking, “How can I help my team become capable of solving this without me?”

The objective isn’t to become less supportive. It’s to make support developmental rather than dependency-producing.

Entrepreneurship is rarely an individual achievement, even when one person’s name appears on the company.

Business partners, spouses, colleagues, suppliers and professional peers often carry consequences of entrepreneurial decisions.

Yet these relationships can receive whatever attention remains after urgent business demands.

The American Psychological Association’s 2024 Work in America survey found that 43% of workers reported typically feeling tense or stressed during the workday, rising to 61% among those experiencing lower psychological safety.

Although those findings aren’t specific to entrepreneurs, they illustrate why healthy working relationships deserve deliberate attention.

Carrying across means collaborating rather than controlling, communicating rather than assuming and recognizing that your success affects people who don’t report to you.

Ask yourself: Which important relationship is receiving the leftovers of my time, energy and attention?

Entrepreneurs can become so consumed with immediate demands that they neglect the future they’re supposedly building.

Carry Forward involves preparing for what comes next: succession, organizational resilience, financial security, leadership development and the legacy of the business.

Imagine two founders operating similarly profitable companies.

One remains involved in every significant decision. The other invests in systems, develops successors and builds a leadership team capable of operating independently.

Both may be successful today, but only one is deliberately reducing the company’s dependence on its founder.

Carrying forward requires moving beyond the question, “What does my business need from me today?”

It asks, “What must I build today, so the business and the people connected to it can thrive tomorrow?”

This may be the most overlooked responsibility of entrepreneurship.

Carry Within concerns the physical, mental and emotional capacity required to sustain everything else.

A founder can become so identified with the business that personal well-being feels secondary to professional achievement.

Sleep becomes negotiable. Exercise gets postponed. Family time becomes conditional. Recovery feels like something to earn after the next milestone.

But your business cannot continually draw from capacity you never replenish.

Carrying within isn’t about avoiding hard work. It’s about recognizing that the entrepreneur is part of the enterprise’s long-term sustainability.

If your business succeeds only while your health, relationships and sense of purpose deteriorate, it’s worth questioning what success actually means.

The Five Carries aren’t five additional responsibilities to pile onto an already crowded calendar. They’re five lenses for evaluating the responsibilities you already have.

Start with a simple exercise. Write down your biggest current obligations and identify which carry each belongs to. Then ask three questions:

What am I carrying? What am I going to carry? What am I finally ready to stop carrying?

You may discover that some responsibilities require greater attention, others need to be delegated and a few should never have remained yours in the first place.

Entrepreneurship will always involve responsibility. The goal isn’t to build a life without weight.

It’s to develop the judgment to carry what matters, share what shouldn’t be carried alone and release what no longer serves the future you’re building.

Because the ultimate measure of entrepreneurial success shouldn’t simply be how much you’ve managed to carry.

It should be what you’ve built, who you’ve helped and whether you still have the human capacity to enjoy it.

Entrepreneurs are often praised for their ability to carry enormous responsibility. They build companies, manage employees, serve customers, make payroll and navigate uncertainty, sometimes all before lunch.

In the beginning, carrying everything can feel necessary. You become the salesperson, marketer, accountant and customer service department because there’s nobody else to do it.

But something changes as the business grows. The responsibilities multiply, and the habits that helped you survive the startup phase can become obstacles to sustainable success.
