#5480. Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned.

The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.”

According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.”

The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space.

In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics.

The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website.

During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.”

But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash.

“We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.”

Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence.

Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake.

“I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.”

Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon, including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities.

But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity.

Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.”

At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.

Yu said the scope of these problems, and the pace at which new ones popped up — almost weekly — made it difficult to give customers reliable updates about why their bikes were delayed.

“The entire team is like running at a million miles an hour to get these things produced and shipped to customers, and then it’s also really dynamic as well,” he said. “I think what we could have done better is just [say], straight up: ‘We’re chasing down these things, we’ll have an update shortly.’”

That didn’t happen at first, but Also has steadily improved its communication, earning some goodwill from customers on Reddit. The company will need it as it works through the inevitable kinks that come with a first product. Early customers have already reported problems, including delivery damage and noticeable battery drain.

#5478. Crypto Stocks Edge Up Before the Bell as 50 Companies Now Block Tokenized Shares: What Is Happening in the Market?

Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Crypto stocks edged higher before Tuesday’s open, November 3, even as Nvidia, Costco and Nike joined the companies blocking tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, taking the count to 50, and an AI chip sell-off sent Seoul’s Kospi down 3.6%.

The bounce is small, and it follows a bad month. Coinbase traded at $138.74 at 13:00 UTC, up 0.7% from Monday’s close of $137.83, its lowest finish since February 2024. Robinhood, Strategy and Circle rose between 0.5% and 1.1%, and Galaxy led with 2.8% after losing 8.8% on Monday.

The bigger story for the sector is the pushback against tokenization. Objectors to OKXICE, the 24/7 venue for tokenized US stocks that OKX is building with NYSE owner ICE, went from 16 to 50 in 11 days. Today is the deadline for companies notified on October 4, so the list could still grow, while Coinbase, Robinhood and the other crypto names on it have yet to say no.

Asia offered no lift. After a 1.1% drop in the Nasdaq on Monday, Samsung and SK hynix dragged the Kospi to 5,648.79, Shanghai slipped 0.8%, and Tokyo was shut for a holiday. Only Hong Kong closed higher, and Bitcoin held steady through the session at $77,326.

Investors are DUMPING US tech stocks at a rapid pace:The Nasdaq 100 index has dropped -6.1% over the last 3 trading sessions, its biggest 3-day decline since the April 2025 Liberation Day selloff. $QQQ This also marks the 3rd-largest 3-day decline since the 2022 bear market.… pic.twitter.com/jNvmex3HZj

So why are so many companies saying no to tokenization, and why are markets red from Seoul to New York?

Because they would carry the risk and see little of the benefit. OKXICE, the venue OKX is building with NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange, wants to offer round-the-clock trading of US stocks as tokens, paid for in stablecoins.

Under the SEC’s exemption, a company can keep its shares off such a venue if an outside firm does the tokenizing. It has 30 days from notice to object, and the objections have come fast:

The newest 12 are Nvidia, Costco, Micron, CrowdStrike, Corning, IREN, USA Rare Earth, Bloom Energy, Nike, Palo Alto Networks, Reddit and Hewlett Packard Enterprise. They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, which runs its own blockchain unit and says it still likes the technology.

The fight is over shareholder rights, especially votes. “Right now companies like Goldman and Microsoft see all of the risk and none of the upside,” Injective’s COO Mirza Uddin told CNBC.

OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo isn’t backing down. “We are at the very beginning of the rollout of fundamentally different market structure,” he said at the October 30 press conference.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

Only the crypto names avoided objection to tokenisation, along with several major US stocks. Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle, Strategy, BitGo and Securitize remain outside the objection list, as do Apple, Amazon, Tesla, SpaceX and Netflix.

One crypto-born company did say no. IREN, the Bitcoin miner that now earns more from renting computers to AI firms than from mining, objected in the latest batch.

Silence isn’t a yes, though. Venues get up to five business days to publish objections, so companies that answered this week may not show up until next week’s notice, and staying off the list doesn’t guarantee a stock will trade at launch.

The AI trade is cracking again. Big Tech results last week showed Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft will keep spending heavily on data centres and chips, and investors want to see faster returns first.

Monday’s selling on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq fell 1.1%, hit Asia’s chipmakers on Tuesday:

Seoul’s slide is the one to watch. The Kospi closed at a record 9,114.55 on June 22 and is now 38% lower, with 17% of that lost since the end of September.

Oil added to the strain. Brent climbed 1.7% to $106.58 after reports of limited US strikes on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after it fell more than 7% on hopes of new talks.

Hong Kong’s crypto stocks split. Exchange operator OSL rose 0.4%, and Boyaa Interactive, which holds Bitcoin, fell 5.1%.

They have been sold off with tech, then sold again for crypto. Every big name is down at least 12% since the end of September, and the first trading day after the Binance hack was the worst of the run.

Coinbase’s daily chart shows how far the slide has gone. The stock is $34 under its 50-day average and more than $50 under its 200-day, and Monday’s close was the lowest since February 2024.

COIN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

The tokenization fight won’t move share prices on its own. For crypto stocks, today’s pre-market bounce still has to survive Wall Street’s open and a long night of election results.

#5474. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5471. A YC startup is putting $1M behind 5 unsolved materials science problems for AI

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Discovered Materials, a months-old San Francisco startup using AI models to find new substances for building advanced chips, announced a million-dollar challenge for AI models to solve five critical problems in materials science.

While frontier AI models have solved a remarkable series of outstanding mathematics problems and made progress in the life sciences, they have yet to truly plumb the complex physics in advanced materials.

“It’s more difficult to specify problems clearly in materials science because it’s not like math, where you have a very specific definition and can get to a yes or no,” said Advaith Sridhar, a co-founder of Discovered Materials, which was part of Y Combinator’s spring 2026 batch. “We came to this discussion [wondering], what are the grand challenges in this field? How do we know AI is making progress?”

Though materials science doesn’t have an equivalent of the Millennium Prize Problems, Discovered Materials recruited an advisory group of academics at leading global universities to spell out five open problems. The company is offering a pool of prizes, worth $1 million in total, for solutions to the problems.

“Across materials science, there are phenomena we observe but cannot explain,” Felipe Jornada, a Stanford professor who helped develop the challenges, said in a statement. “Explaining these phenomena would improve our understanding of physics, and the answers would directly shape how we build electronics, store energy, and manufacture the materials of the future.”

Before announcing the challenges, Discovered Materials turned frontier lab models loose on them, giving AI agents internet access and other resources to work autonomously for days. The models spent several days on each problem without making much headway. Still, it’s easy to imagine OpenAI or Anthropic attempting to one-shot them with significantly more compute or a newer model.

“It’s not particularly a concern to us whether we find it, or someone else finds it, or a professor finds it, or the frontier labs find it,” Sridhar said. “The reason we’re putting out these challenges is because we want them to serve as the goalposts. If you go and solve these challenges, we are deepening our understanding of materials and how things around us behave.”

Tracking efforts to solve the problems will show “whether the models are climbing in this domain,” he added.

The challenge also reflects the changing nature of scientific inquiry as AI proves capable of uncovering insights and techniques human researchers didn’t anticipate. With solutions apparently easier to find than ever, the questions become more important.

“This is a new way of thinking about science, where we come up with the verification and the challenges first, and then we let somebody come up with the ideas that explain the problem,” Sridhar said. “Knowing what are the right questions to ask is not trivial and very difficult in this domain, so this is where the professors have really helped us shape what are the right questions we should be asking.”

Discovered Materials’ main focus is developing new materials for use in semiconductors; the startup partners with chip giants on research projects while also funding its own scientific efforts. When the company announced its seed round in August, Sridhar told TechCrunch that he hoped the company would generate a useful material within a year.

“Those timelines have accelerated a little bit,” he says today. “I’m more confident now that we will be able to find these industrially useful materials in a timeline shorter than a year.”

Beyond official gold purchases, several major global developments could strengthen the broader precious metals market. A lasting resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict could free up capital and reduce certain risk premiums, while still allowing for ongoing monetary and geopolitical uncertainties that favor hard assets.

A permanent ceasefire between Iran and the United States, along with normalized shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, could help lower energy-driven inflation spikes. This situation might also encourage central banks to maintain accommodative policies longer.

However, things aren’t looking too great in either Ukraine or the Middle East, with Russia bombing civilians as recently as yesterday, while Iran and the US continue to attack one another, making any hopes of a ceasefire seem a long way off.

Other supporting factors include growing concerns about the stability of fiat currencies, ongoing de-dollarization trends among major economies, high fiscal deficits in key nations, and a clear shift by major central banks towards more aggressive monetary easing.

Historically, these factors have led to increased demand for gold and silver as safe-haven assets.

In this speculative scenario, if favorable global conditions for hard assets continue, gold could potentially reach a price range of $8,000 to $12,000 per troy ounce, with a stretch target exceeding $15,000 by January 1, 2027.

However, it’s important to emphasize that this is purely speculation and should not be considered a realistic base-case outlook.

Achieving this price would require extraordinary coordination among various central banks and sovereign entities, which is currently highly unlikely.

#5468. Aina’s smart ring has a screen, a joystick, and a mic so you can talk to AI agents

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.

The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July, is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.

The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.

Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.

Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01, Sandbar Stream, Oasis, and Natura, which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.

For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.

I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format, with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.

It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.

“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.

Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller. The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.

Aina’s ring goes on preorder starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.

Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.

Zipline and Walmart reached a new multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.

On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.

The company, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, said it plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.

Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based company began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.

But it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.

Zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.

The company said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

#5466. Axiom Math wants to keep AI slop out of mathematics

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

It feels like AI is cracking a new math problem every week. Last month, OpenAI released 719 manuscriptsclaiming solutions to some of the field’s hardest problems. But even the computer checks meant to confirm those results can slip. After years of AI slop, it’s fair to wonder whether math is next.

Axiom Math is betting math can avoid that fate, not by slowing down, but by standing on firmer ground. The $1.6 billion startup wants to build a verified foundation that AI agents can rely on to write software and, eventually, do science.

On Wednesday, the company announced it had formally verified the Stacks Project, one of the largest bodies of mathematics ever written by humans. Mathematicians often hold Stacks in rare regard — Columbia mathematician Peter Woit has claimed there’s “nothing else really comparable,” comparing the project to “the famous Bourbaki books,” a series that rebuilt math from its foundations in the 20th century.

Woit’s Columbia colleague Johan de Jong started the Stacks Project in 2005 as an open source reference. Mathematicians have contributed to it ever since, building out results from college-level algebra all the way up to the field’s most advanced ideas across algebra, geometry, and number theory.

The company’s fleet of AI agents translates the library’s roughly 7,654 pages into about 16 million lines of computer-checked code.

Formalizing math is a way of making sure the structure underneath it is sound. Mathematicians rewrite the proof as code in a programming language called Lean, and a program called a proof assistant checks the code line by line. If the proof passes, mathematicians can trust that it’s logically sound.

Engineers use the same idea, called formal verification, to confirm their chip designs work, while researchers in France have used it to catch bugs in software that calculates family benefits.

For a library like the Stacks Project, checking each theorem is only part of the job. The theorems and definitions in Stacks are interconnected, and each one builds on the ones before it. Like a family tree, many results in Stacks trace back to the ones that came before it.

That interconnectedness made Axiom unsure the project would work at first. The team had to keep every connection intact across about 16 million lines of Lean code.

“Things that are big and things that are delicate in life just don’t go together,” Axiom CEO Carina Hong told TechCrunch. “[Stacks] is a collection of mathematical results that is the foundation of mathematics. You want [theorems] to be consistent and not, like, paradoxical. You want the definitions to not fight with each other.”

The 25-year-old CEO dropped out of a Stanford math PhD program and founded the company in March 2025. In March, Axiom raised a $200 million Series A led by Menlo Ventures.

“We were not sure if vibe coding would be able to preserve the beauty of Stacks,” Hong said.

To pull off the project, the team gave its agents a loose structure and let them run in parallel. “With Stacks, we imposed a hierarchy … [but] it was not, like, a complete hierarchy of dictating what every single agent was doing,” said Ashvin Swaminathan, a member of Axiom’s technical staff. “The agents were finding tasks for themselves and identified things that they could work on in parallel.”

Axiom also trained its own models to be good at math, an approach Hong said most other verification startups haven’t taken. At first, the team relied on one of its in-house Lean experts to teach the agents a human sense of taste. Over time, Hong said, the agents have picked up taste on their own.

The result fills one of the biggest gaps in formalized math. “When you look at what has been formalized in mathematics, there’s this huge black hole. And that black hole covers algebraic geometry,” Swaminathan said.

Until now, researchers who wanted to check new work in algebraic geometry with Lean had little to build on, Swaminathan said. “Well, now they do.”

Axiom argues that each verified result becomes a building block, so future proofs can lean on checked math instead of starting from scratch. Terence Tao, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medal winner, has made the general case more simply: “The more formalized proofs you have, the more formalized proofs you can make.”

Mathematicians aren’t Axiom’s only intended audience. Developers have long struggled to guarantee that their code is free of bugs and security holes. That problem grows as AI agents write more of the world’s code.

Axiom is betting that the software of the future will need to rest on verified foundations, the way Stacks now does.

“We believe that mathematics is the domain where you start building these things and that it’s a transferable skill,” Swaminathan said. “Agents can read our code, understand it, and build new infrastructure on top of it. Our Lean formalization is now the substrate that agents can build upon.”

The way Axiom’s agents built Stacks, working in parallel and picking their own tasks, is how Hong expects much of AI’s future work to happen. AI agents, she argues, will need a well-built, reusable body of knowledge to keep from producing slop.

“You want [agents] to have a reusable library for them to build on and keep pushing the frontier,” Hong said. “If you slop drop in a way that’s bad engineering choices in the beginning, then it’s very hard for them to grow that boundary.”

Hong is confident enough in that approach to issue a dare. “I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale.”

Food delivery startup Wonder is moving closer to becoming a publicly traded company after confidentially filing for an initial public offering (IPO). The company announced the filing on Thursday, marking a major milestone following years of fundraising, acquisitions, and expansion.

Wonder has yet to reveal how many shares it plans to make available or the expected price range.

#5464. Binance Says Its $6.3 Billion Hack Began With a Fake Job Interview, but Traders Aren’t Convinced

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Binance said on Tuesday, November 3, that the Binance hack started with a fake job interview, in which North Korean hackers gave one of its engineers a coding test laced with malware, but many traders still doubt that is the whole story.

The October 29 theft took $6.34 billion from Binance’s hot wallets, the largest crypto heist on record. Binance’s incident report describes a campaign that ran for months: a tampered download in June, the fake interview in September and an internal AI tool that led the attackers to the engineers who ran its wallets.

Not everyone is buying it. Since the hack, traders on X have called it an inside job. They point to how fast the money left, across ten blockchains in about 20 minutes, and to how often Binance’s account has changed.

BREAKING: Binance says hackers used a fake job interview to infect an employee's computer.The malware let them hijack Binance's internal AI tool, take over more engineers' accounts, and drain $6.34 billion from its hot wallets.

No one has offered proof. The FBI has tied the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, and blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs agrees with high confidence.

BNB hasn’t recovered either. It trades at $703.33, up 0.7% today but still 7.4% below its $759.85 close the day before the hack.

So what exactly does Binance say happened, and why are traders still unconvinced?

Slowly, through three engineers. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC the attackers “spent months building their way in” and rejected the idea that a single laptop was the weak point.

“This wasn’t one mistake or one breach – it was a months-long campaign,” Teng wrote on X.

Binance says users won’t lose anything. It has replaced 98% of the stolen assets with its own funds, and about $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted with the help of Tether, Circle and others.

Discover: Bitcoin Settles Its $10.9 Billion Options Expiry Right on Max Pain After the Binance Hack

Because the doubts started before the report, and the report didn’t settle them. Two days after the theft, trader Financelancelot called it “totally an inside job,” and Solana trader Ansem wrote: “My trust in binance is gone.”

The skeptics keep coming back to five points:

The proof of reserves didn’t help. Binance’s November 2 proof used an October 31 snapshot, taken after it had already bought back most of the stolen coins, so critics say it can’t show how big the hole was.

A hack of this scale means serious security failures occurred. No platform is unhackable, but that cannot be an excuse. Every incident exposes weaknesses that should have been prevented.Some details are embarrassing. Public explanations also simplify what appears to have been a… https://t.co/ZMAjZt2hF8

Some of the louder claims have already fallen apart. A viral post blaming a North Korean “honey trap” passed 800,000 views before co-founder Yi He called it untrue and said ZachXBT, the investigator it quoted, never said it.

An employee’s laptop being the way in doesn’t make it an inside job. Fake job offers with booby-trapped coding tests are TraderTraitor’s best-known trick, the same group behind the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025.

Less than half of it has been stopped. Of the $6.34 billion taken, Binance says $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted, much of it stablecoins that Tether and Circle could lock.

The rest is on the move. Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic counts about $3.24 billion still in addresses linked to the attackers, and Chainalysis has found the stolen funds mixed with money from September’s Bitget exploit.

One pile hasn’t moved at all. The 233.46 million XRP taken from Binance, worth about $299 million, has sat in six wallets since November 2, untouched as of Wednesday morning.

Discover: Bitcoin Sellers Take a Week of Losses Below $80,000 as Strategy and Strive Keep Buying: Will $75,000 Hold?

More proof, and soon. Three things are due in the next few days:

Not yet. BNB fell 8.1% on October 29, from $759.85 to $698.46, on $414 million in volume, more than four times what it traded the day before.

It has leaned on its 200-day EMA ever since. BNB dipped to $680.74 earlier today, close to the $680 hack low, and bounced back to $703.33.

Binance has told its version of the Binance hack in detail. Until the independent review backs it up, traders will keep reading BNB’s chart as a vote of confidence.

#5462. As Binance Battles $6.3B Hack Fallout, Coinbase Reveals 99% of Customer Crypto Assets Are in Cold Storage

Questions about the safety of funds held on centralized exchanges have resurfaced following one of the crypto industry’s most alarming security incidents. As investors reassess the risks of keeping their holdings on trading platforms, Coinbase, America’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, is moving to reassure customers that its security measures make it harder for a similar breach to occur on its platform.

The platform is highlighting a key part of its protection strategy, disclosing that more than 99% of customer assets are kept in cold storage, with only a small fraction exposed to online systems. The disclosure offers a glimpse into how Coinbase approaches asset protection amid heightened scrutiny of exchange security.

Coinbase says its approach to safeguarding customer funds goes beyond simply keeping most holdings offline. The exchange maintains that over 99% of customer assets are stored in cold wallets, while distributed private keys, withdrawal restrictions, and systems designed to detect unusual activity provide additional layers of protection against unauthorized transactions.

In a blog post published Wednesday, Coinbase also clarified that it was not impacted by the Binance security incident. The exchange emphasized that customer holdings are maintained on a 1:1 basis and remain the property of their owners. It added that these assets are neither lent out nor used without customer authorization.

Beyond its cold-storage strategy, Coinbase outlines several additional security measures designed to give customers greater control over their accounts. According to its security page, the exchange supports two-factor authentication and hardware security keys, while its Coinbase Vault feature adds another layer of protection by allowing users to require multiple approvals before withdrawals can be completed.

Coinbase stressed that security remains an ongoing priority as emerging technologies reshape the threat landscape. The exchange said its responsibility is to keep “improving safeguards” and “continuously monitor for threats” to protect customers. It also pointed to the rapid advancement of AI, noting that it is changing the security environment and making continued investment in “best-in-class security innovation” increasingly important.

Coinbase also maintains a separation between customer holdings and its own corporate assets, reinforcing the distinction between funds belonging to users and those controlled by the company. In its latest quarterly filing, the exchange disclosed that its platform held approximately $377 billion in assets. By comparison, Coinbase reported $8.6 billion in corporate cash and another $2.2 billion in crypto assets held on its own balance sheet.

Coinbase’s statement comes days after the October 29 Binance heist, which saw approximately $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from the exchange’s internet-connected hot wallets. In an update posted Wednesday, Binance announced that it had replenished 98% of the affected assets using its own funds. The exchange also expanded its proof-of-reserves coverage to include 44 cryptocurrencies, highlighting its efforts to reassure customers about the security and backing of their holdings.

In a separate incident, Brazilian cryptocurrency exchange Mercado Bitcoin also suspended withdrawals following a reported $45 million hack, adding to growing concerns about the security of centralized trading platforms.

#5461. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5458. Hong Kong Passes Its Crypto Tax Reporting Law: Exchanges Must Collect User Data From 2027 and Share It Abroad From 2028

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Hong Kong lawmakers passed a crypto tax reporting law on Wednesday, November 4, requiring crypto platforms tied to the city to collect their users’ tax details from 2027, so tax officials can share them with other countries from 2028.

The law brings in the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, or CARF, the global standard for tracing crypto gains across borders. The government said Hong Kong’s Inland Revenue Department will start exchanging the data with partner jurisdictions in 2028.

The same bill updates the Common Reporting Standard, the system banks already use to report foreign accounts. Its new version, which also covers digital financial products, takes effect in 2028.

Hong Kong isn’t moving alone. It is one of 27 jurisdictions, including Singapore, the UAE and Switzerland, that have committed to first exchanges by 2028, the OECD’s latest list shows. Another 46, including the UK, the EU and Japan, start a year earlier.

So what does the new law ask of crypto platforms, and what changes for traders who use them?

It turns crypto platforms into tax reporters. The Inland Revenue Department’s CARF guide calls them reporting crypto-asset service providers: any business that carries out crypto trades for customers, whether as an exchange, a broker, a dealer or a crypto ATM operator.

A platform falls under Hong Kong’s rules if it is tax resident in the city, incorporated there, managed from there, or runs a branch or regular place of business there. Every platform that meets one of those tests has to register with the department, even if it has nothing to report.

Existing customers aren’t exempt. Platforms get 12 months after the rules take effect to collect self-certifications from users who already have accounts.

The law also sets offences for failing to register, skipping due diligence or filing wrong returns. Users can be prosecuted too, for knowingly or recklessly giving false information in a self-certification.

“Hong Kong has been supporting international efforts in enhancing tax transparency and combatting cross-border tax evasion,” said Christopher Hui, Hong Kong’s Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury.

Discover: Franklin Templeton Readies Two ETFs That Turn Stock Dividends Into Bitcoin as Washington Writes Crypto Rules Without Congress

On January 1, 2027, less than two months away. The bill moved quickly: a public consultation ran from December 2025 to February 2026, and the government published the bill on May 22.

Platforms that first fall under the rules in 2027 have until January 31, 2028, to register. The department hasn’t yet published the details of its online portal or the data format it wants.

Hong Kong is in the second wave. The OECD’s commitments list, last updated on September 14, splits the world like this:

Hong Kong’s rivals for crypto business are on the same schedule. Singapore and the UAE have also committed to their first exchanges by 2028.

Existing users will get the same request within a year. Lying on it is an offence under the new law, so ticking the wrong country isn’t a way around it.

That is usually enough for a tax office to spot crypto gains that never showed up on a return. Transfers to outside wallets are covered too, so moving coins off the exchange still leaves a record.

Platforms carry the heavier load. They have under two months to build the forms, the checks and the records, and the department has yet to publish its portal details.

For traders, Hong Kong’s crypto tax law closes one of the last big Asian gaps in the OECD’s reporting net. By 2028, a crypto account in Hong Kong, Singapore or Dubai will be about as visible to a home tax office as a bank account.

#5456. Why Coinbase Bitcoin Discount Just Hit a Yearly High

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Classic crypto market metrics have suddenly stopped reflecting reality. Bitcoin’s discount on the U.S. exchange Coinbase relative to the international Binance has hit a yearly high, with the Coinbase Premium Index collapsing to around −0.06%.

In normal times, such a chart gives traders a cold sweat: the index going deep into the red zone means that large funds in the U.S. have started massively dumping crypto.

However, the current collapse of the indicator turned out to be a technical illusion. It was provoked by the emergency freeze of operations on Binance immediately after a large-scale hack of the exchange, which completely blocked classic cross-exchange arbitrage.

The anomalous price gap coincided with the largest incident in the industry’s history: on October 29–30, hackers attacked Binance’s hot wallets, withdrawing about $6.3 billion. The exchange promptly froze half of the stolen funds on the blockchain, and the head of the platform promised to fully cover the remaining client losses from the SAFU reserve fund.

Nevertheless, amid the panic, the price of Bitcoin dropped to $77,000–$78,000.

To localize the problem, Binance completely shut the gateways — it temporarily banned any deposits and withdrawals of funds. This decision instantly paralyzed cross-exchange arbitrage. Large players physically could not buy the temporarily cheaper Bitcoin on Coinbase and transfer it to Binance to even out the price.

Liquidity was locked inside the platforms, which caused the discount to artificially swell to its widest level in a year.

As noted by Galaxy Research’s head of research Alex Thorn, due to the blocking of transactions, the discount on Coinbase temporarily stopped being a signal of weak demand in the U.S.

On November 1, Binance announced a phased reopening of withdrawals, starting with BTC and ETH. Now the market is waiting to see how quickly arbitrageurs eliminate the gap. If the gap closes in the coming days, it means the anomaly was purely technical.

If the negative spread becomes entrenched, it will be an alarming signal of a real cooling of American capital.

#5453. Hackers Use Claude, Gemini and Kimi to Identify Valuable Crypto Targets

Cybercriminals are using popular artificial intelligence (AI) models like Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and Moonshot AI's Kimi AI to evaluate the financial worth of potential victims, including those owning cryptocurrencies.

Cybersecurity researchers at Cisco Talos detailed in a new report how a new type of Windows malware dubbed VOLTA-AUTODOXER, or simply VOLTA, steals sensitive data and uses AI tools to identify potentially lucrative targets among compromised users.

Compared to traditional information-stealing malware, which mainly steals passwords and credentials, VOLTA can also analyze stolen data to build victim profiles and determine what assets hackers can potentially exploit for profit.

Notably, one of VOLTA's most dangerous features is its ability to extract sensitive crypto wallet information, including recovery seed phrases, which can potentially give attackers access to digital assets.

VOLTA also includes features that can crack cryptocurrency wallet vaults, posing a big risk for people who store their crypto wallet credentials on their computers.

But its features are not just limited to stealing crypto.

As explained by Cisco Talos security researcher Ryan Fetterman, VOLTA can also grab saved browser passwords, payment card info, authentication tokens, email credentials and active sessions on popular platforms like Telegram, Discord, Steam and Roblox.

It can also extract info from Outlook accounts and Slack workspaces, as well as other personal and professional information on the infected system.

The malware also takes things further by analyzing victims' email accounts to grab more personal data.

For example, it can scan Gmail accounts for purchase confirmations and receipts from services like Amazon, PayPal, Walmart, DoorDash and Uber Eats.

This way, attackers can get more details about a victim's identity, home address, job and spending habits.

The malware can send stolen data to AI models via the OpenRouter service, which provides access to several AI models.

It first tries to process the collected data using Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6.

If the model fails to process the request, VOLTA is hardcoded to try Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.

As explained by Cisco Talos, VOLTA specifically looks for refusal responses before attempting to use a different AI model.

It feeds the collected data to the AI models and asks them to analyze it, providing a comprehensive evaluation of a victim's financial worth.

It can also help identify valuable assets and then rank them based on how lucrative they may be. It can also score a victim's cybersecurity.

Essentially, it allows hackers to use AI models to find potentially lucrative targets without the need to manually sift through stolen data.

“This deleveraging dynamic is a rather positive signal as it suggests that pressure on XRP futures is gradually easing,” the analyst said.

Moreover, Darkfost cited previous episodes in which falling open interest preceded substantial XRP rallies, suggesting a similar scenario could unfold.

“We saw this in mid-September, when XRP gained 32% in the following period, and after the mid-August episode, which was followed by a 72% rally.” He added.

Martinez also identified a potential technical catalyst for a rebound. The analyst said the TD Sequential indicator had flashed a buy signal on XRP’s three-day chart, noting that the previous three comparable signals preceded rebounds of 31%, 24% and 18%. However, the setup depends on XRP holding its support level.

“Hold it, and XRP could rebound toward $1.40. Lose it while whales continue taking profits, and $0.98 could be next,” Martinez said.

Elsewhere, analyst Joep Gerla highlighted XRP’s prolonged consolidation as a possible precursor to a larger advance. He compared the current price structure with previous consolidation periods that preceded rallies of 63,617% in 2017–2018, 1,687% in 2020–2021 and 901% in 2024–2025.

“XRP has been in prolonged consolidation, a structure that has preceded major expansion phases in previous cycles,” Gerla wrote. “The edge goes to those who stay patient before the breakout.”

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The compromised hot wallet of the Binance exchange has been completely emptied. Blockchain tracker Whale Alert recorded two identical transactions of 40 million XRP each (around $101 million in total), which went to a new address 50 seconds apart.

This is the platform's corporate address rK21t6nGLy4MNDqhvy3pGwcLFy25qgfzMx. After the October 29 attack, the wallet received an official red "Reported as hacked" label in network explorers.

As a result of this final transfer, the address's balance dropped to 23.7 XRP (around $30) — the exchange fully removed the remaining funds, moving them to new internal wallets.

This transfer effectively closes activity on the vulnerable address and is a planned technical consolidation of the remaining balances. The transfer of assets followed a large-scale cross-chain attack on Binance that began on October 29. Total damage across ten different blockchains is estimated at $6.3 billion, making the incident the largest crypto theft in history.

Hot wallets on the XRP Ledger took the first hit: within five minutes at the start of the attack, a total of 233.46 million XRP (around $296 million) was withdrawn from them.

The specifics of the XRPL network itself oblige the exchange to fully zero out hacked addresses. Unlike most stablecoins (such as USDT or USDC), where issuers can forcibly freeze funds, the XRP Ledger code has no protocol-level blocking function.

Neither Ripple nor independent XRP Ledger developers has no technical ability to stop transactions, so leaving any available balance on a hacked wallet is unsafe. Moving the remaining 80 million XRP to new wallets isolated by the platform eliminates the risk of repeated withdrawals.

For the XRP ecosystem, this incident became an absolute all-time negative record, surpassing the September hack of the Bitget exchange, in which 103 million XRP ($157 million) was lost, multiple times over.

At the same time, no panic has been recorded on the market. Binance has fully restored withdrawal operations for clients. The platform's management officially stated that all net user losses will be compensated 1:1 from corporate reserves and SAFU fund money.

The transfer of the last $101 million in XRP likely puts an end to operations with the hacked address, minimizing further technical risks for the platform.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. The XRP Ledger (XRPL) is set for a significant week ahead as its long-awaited cleanup upgrade heads for mainnet activation this week, bringing a wide-ranging collection of fixes and improvements to the blockchain.

The fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment, a collection of fixes for Single Asset Vaults, the Lending Protocol, Automated Market Makers, the permissioned DEX, trust lines, NFTs, MPTs, Escrow, Sponsorship, transaction signing, and permission delegation, is at the center of attention, with validator support putting it on track for a potential November 4 activation, provided the required voting threshold of 80% is sustained.

The earliest activation date is Nov 4, 2026 at 2:46 PM UTC, with just 2 days left according to the xrpscan countdown timer.

Some tokens on the XRP Ledger are supposed to be stored in accounts approved by their issuer; however, developers have found a few ways around that rule.

Issuers of regulated assets, such as stablecoins or tokenized funds, can require approval before anyone holds their tokens, typically to perform identity checks first.

Four proposed code changes would resolve the remaining exceptions. All four are included in a single network upgrade dubbed fixCleanup3_5_0.

These have not been merged into the XRP Ledger's main software yet. Once they are, fixCleanup3_5_0 requires support from more than 80% of the network's trusted validators for two weeks before being activated.

According to Hussein Zangana (Vet), director of community at XRP Ledger Foundation, there is a critical Linux kernel vulnerability on kernels 4.4+, affecting any unpatched Linux server in the world with an open IPv4 TCP port. For XRP Ledger node and validator operators who run RHEL 8/9/10, Debian 12/13, Amazon Linux, and Oracle UEK, a fix has already been shipped; they are simply expected to update and reboot.

For those who run Ubuntu, AlmaLinux, Rocky, CentOS Stream, this might not suffice, as they may need to take further steps until a fix is shipped for their distro. They should re-apply the nft rule after a reboot or a flush ruleset reload.

The contrasting developments put Hong Kong’s growing digital asset industry in focus. While American investors reduce exposure through listed products, Asian financial institutions are building new ways to access Bitcoin.

US spot Bitcoin ETF products recorded $430.2 million in net outflows on November 5. Fidelity’s FBTC led withdrawals with $199.9 million, followed by BlackRock’s IBIT at $105 million. Grayscale’s GBTC recorded another $49.9 million in withdrawals, while Franklin Templeton’s EZBC lost $32.9 million.

The latest session pushed November’s cumulative Bitcoin ETFs outflows to $869.8 million across four trading sessions. Net withdrawals across the latest seven finalized sessions reached approximately $1.36 billion.

That pressure follows a brief recovery on November 4, when the funds attracted $74.6 million. However, the latest withdrawals suggest institutional demand remains fragile.

The selling also comes as Bitcoin struggles to regain momentum. Investors are now watching if continued redemptions translate into further pressure on the underlying market.

Hong Kong’s wider asset management industry reached HK$42.2 trillion, according to the Securities and Futures Commission. This gives traditional financial institutions a substantial pool of capital from which to develop new investment products.

The longer-term opportunity extends beyond immediate Bitcoin ETF subscriptions. Hong Kong is developing an institutional ecosystem that includes regulated products, custody services, and established wealth management firms.

The latest US withdrawals show that institutional demand can reverse quickly. However, Hong Kong’s expanding infrastructure displays that the competition for digital asset capital across global financial centers is far from over.

#5445. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

The latest on-chain data puts SHIB exchange reserves at 85.8432 trillion tokens, up only 0.01% over the past 24 hours. The seven-day chart tells a different story: reserves have fallen noticeably, which suggests a lot of SHIB has left trading platforms.

Lower exchange reserves generally mean fewer tokens are on hand to be sold. When investors pull SHIB into private wallets, there is less supply available to sellers on centralized exchanges. That doesn't guarantee a price recovery, but it can make the supply picture more favorable.

The reserves are currently valued at about $397.45 million, down 1.69% on the day. Exchange netflow is still positive at roughly 10.94 billion SHIB, so short-term selling pressure hasn't gone away.

The supply picture is improving, but the chart is still bearish. On the daily SHIB/USDT chart, the token trades near $0.00000463 after breaking below its ascending support trendline. It is also under several important moving averages, which means sellers still control the broader structure.

Immediate resistance sits around $0.00000500–$0.00000530. The $0.00000440–$0.00000450 region is the next potential support zone.

If demand starts to recover, the drop in exchange-held supply could matter more. For now, the 85 trillion mark is a constructive on-chain sign, not a confirmed bullish reversal. A more convincing case would need continued exchange withdrawals, stronger buying, and a move back above the key resistance levels.

An unknown investor has built a position in Zcash (ZEC) worth about $14 million, splitting the capital between the spot market and the decentralized derivatives exchange Hyperliquid. The purchases came amid preparations for the Network Upgrade 7 (NU7) hard fork: on November 5, it is set to speed up block processing threefold.

Judging by on-chain data, the address t1JJnA linked to the investor first bought 3,052 ZEC (about $3.8 million) on the spot market at an average price of $1,250. Then, on Hyperliquid, it opened a 2x leveraged long on 8,000 ZEC worth $10.16 million in two different wallets.

So far, 3,000 ZEC of this position can be verified, with an average entry price of $1,353.83.

In late October, ZEC pulled back to the $1,220–$1,280 range, and the derivatives position went into the red. At its peak, the paper loss exceeded $1.8 million; it now stands at $249,388.

But liquidation will only occur if the price falls to $647.67, which is nearly half of current levels. The investor is clearly betting on long-term growth rather than a quick rebound.

The main argument is the NU7 hard fork, whose final tests the developers completed on the testnet in October. The ZIP-218 update will cut block time from 75 to 25 seconds: the network’s throughput will triple, while the issuance schedule will remain the same.

Along with the hard fork, the Network Sustainability Mechanism (a reserve fee fund for miners) will go live, and the outdated Sprout pool will be shut down in favor of the shielded Orchard architecture.

Throughout 2026, each new Zcash low came in higher than the previous one. An ascending triangle has formed on the chart, and time after time the price runs into resistance at $1,396. Traders on the derivatives market have split into two camps.

Some expect a sharp upside breakout amid inflows into the Grayscale Zcash Trust. Others fear that right after the upgrade activates on November 5, the “buy the rumor, sell the news” principle will kick in.
